paragraphs: Classification becomes expensive when a model must assign probabilities across an enormous set of possible classes. Computing the full softmax requires considering that set, creating both computational and energy costs. Negative sampling reduces this work by selecting a smaller collection of incorrect classes, but the usefulness of those samples depends on how they are chosen.

The paper addresses the tension between informative sampling and inexpensive sampling. Ideally, the sampling distribution should respond to the current input, the model's changing parameters, and the correct class. Existing alternatives described in the abstract compromise either this adaptivity or the cost of drawing samples. The authors identify two classes of distributions that support adaptive sampling with a provable near-constant sampling time.

The implementation results connect that theoretical contribution to practical training. In the reported comparison, a C++ implementation running on a CPU achieves better accuracy and wall-clock time than optimized TensorFlow implementations of popular alternatives running on an NVIDIA V100 GPU. This supports the value of the proposed sampling schemes in that comparison, rather than establishing a general advantage of CPUs over GPUs.
icml-2021-a-tale-of-two-efficient-and-in.tldr: Two adaptive negative-sampling distribution families offer provably near-constant sampling time and strong reported accuracy and runtime results.

paragraphs: Variational autoencoders can compress complex data into a lower-dimensional representation, but their decoder is usually a neural network whose behavior is difficult to interpret or constrain. This becomes a problem when a researcher has prior knowledge about how the low-dimensional representation should relate to the original features. A flexible decoder is useful only if that flexibility can coexist with the required structure.

The paper introduces DeVAE, which specifies the decoder through a derivative-based forward mapping. Describing behavior in derivative space gives greater control over how the output changes as the representation changes. The contribution is therefore a different way to construct the decoder, allowing prior knowledge to shape its behavior while retaining an expressive nonlinear mapping.

BasisDeVAE adds a sparse clustering prior to this construction. It combines dimensionality reduction with clustering at the feature level, making both tasks part of an interpretable model. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate performance and scalability for the proposed models. The stated findings support derivative-based decoding as a way to combine expressive representations, interpretable structure, and respect for prior knowledge.
icml-2021-basisdevae-interpretable-simul.tldr: DeVAE controls decoder behavior through derivatives, while BasisDeVAE adds interpretable feature clustering alongside dimensionality reduction.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent can encounter conditions that were absent during training. Robust reinforcement learning addresses this by training against an adversary: the agent seeks a useful policy while the adversary seeks conditions that make its performance worse. This minimax formulation makes reliability an explicit learning objective, but solving it efficiently and at large scale is challenging.

The proposed RH-UCRL algorithm uses a learned model of the environment and distinguishes epistemic uncertainty from aleatoric uncertainty. These correspond to uncertainty about the model and randomness in the environment. It explores the decision spaces of both the agent and the adversary during policy learning, combining the search for informative experience with preparation for unfavorable situations.

The authors provide a theoretical solution with near-optimal sample complexity guarantees. They also scale the approach using ensembles of neural network models and neural network policies. Across the adversarial environments evaluated, RH-UCRL outperforms other robust deep reinforcement learning algorithms. Together, the analysis and experiments support the proposed combination of robust policy learning and efficient exploration.
icml-2021-combining-pessimism-with-optim.tldr: RH-UCRL combines robust policy learning with uncertainty-aware exploration, providing sample complexity guarantees and strong results in adversarial environments.

paragraphs: This paper studies linear regression when an adversary can arbitrarily corrupt most observed responses. A crucial condition is that the adversary chooses the corruption without knowing the design matrix. Only an alpha fraction of observations must remain uncorrupted, so the setting permits the useful observations to be heavily outnumbered.

The authors show that the Huber loss estimator can consistently recover the regression coefficients when n grows faster than d/alpha², where d is the number of coefficients. Its error scales as the square root of d/(alpha²n), with the stated bounds optimal up to constants. The results extend beyond Gaussian designs, provided the design matrix's column span does not contain approximately sparse vectors.

Two proofs explain the result through strong convexity and through a connection to high-dimensional medians. For Gaussian designs, the median connection yields a simple coordinate-wise median algorithm with nearly optimal guarantees and linear runtime; it can also exploit sparse coefficients. The corruption model additionally covers heavy-tailed noise without a first moment, broadening the relevance of the analysis beyond explicitly adversarial data.
icml-2021-consistent-regression-when-obl.tldr: Under an oblivious-corruption model and a design condition, Huber regression remains consistent even when most observations are outliers.

paragraphs: Monte-Carlo Tree Search plans by exploring possible sequences of decisions. It must balance revisiting promising actions against investigating less-explored possibilities. The paper targets the sample and computational costs of this process, including the kind of search used alongside reinforcement learning in AlphaGo and AlphaZero.

The authors introduce a general theoretical framework for convex regularization in tree search. Regularization shapes exploration and policy updates rather than leaving those choices entirely to the usual search rule. Their analysis provides regret guarantees for regularized MCTS and establishes an exponential convergence rate. They then derive new backup operators, which determine how information from explored outcomes updates the search tree, using relative entropy and Tsallis entropy.

The Tsallis-based construction receives stronger theoretical guarantees in their framework. A toy problem illustrates consequences of the analysis, while experiments across several Atari games show advantages over representative baselines. The authors also describe how the framework can be incorporated into AlphaGo. The contribution connects a general mathematical treatment of regularization to concrete changes in how search explores and updates decisions.
icml-2021-convex-regularization-in-monte.tldr: Convex regularization gives Monte-Carlo Tree Search new exploration and update rules with theoretical guarantees and reported Atari improvements.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks build in a preference for local image structure, which helps them learn efficiently from data. Vision transformers offer more flexible attention, but the abstract describes their reliance on expensive external pretraining or distillation from convolutional networks. ConViT investigates whether a transformer can benefit from locality without making that preference a fixed architectural restriction.

Its central mechanism is gated positional self-attention. The attention layers begin by behaving locally, resembling convolutional layers. Each attention head then adjusts a gate that controls the balance between positional information and image content. This lets learning retain locality where it is useful or move beyond it where content-based relationships are more useful.

On ImageNet, ConViT outperforms DeiT and shows substantially improved sample efficiency in the reported experiments. The authors also study how ordinary self-attention encourages locality and how the proposed layers move away from it, alongside ablation experiments examining the architecture. These findings support a soft inductive bias: a useful starting preference that the model can revise during learning.
icml-2021-convit-improving-vision-transf.tldr: ConViT starts transformer attention with a learnable preference for locality, improving ImageNet performance and sample efficiency over DeiT.

paragraphs: Few-shot imitation asks an agent to perform a previously unseen task after seeing only a few demonstrations. This paper trains such agents with demonstration-conditioned reinforcement learning, or DCRL. The policy receives demonstrations as part of its input, allowing the examples to inform which task it should perform.

Training uses multiple tasks with demonstrations, reward functions, and transition distributions. The policy learns to maximize average cumulative reward across those tasks. Because the objective rewards successful behavior, the method can improve on suboptimal demonstrations instead of being limited to reproducing them. The authors also identify the ability to use demonstrations containing only states and to handle a domain shift between demonstrator and agent.

This approach has an explicit requirement: reward functions must be available during training. The paper presents that as a disadvantage relative to earlier methods based on behavior cloning or inferring rewards from demonstrations. In the reported navigation and Meta-World robotic manipulation experiments, DCRL substantially outperforms behavior-cloning methods. The results support using demonstrations to condition a reward-trained policy for few-shot task execution.
icml-2021-demonstration-conditioned-rein.tldr: DCRL trains policies to use demonstrations as task inputs, outperforming behavior cloning while requiring reward functions during training.

paragraphs: Choosing a learning algorithm is itself difficult when the best model class or tuning parameter is unknown. This paper studies that choice in stochastic bandits and reinforcement learning by combining several base algorithms. Each candidate comes with a proposed regret bound, describing its expected performance shortfall, but the framework does not require every proposed bound to be valid.

At each round, a balancing condition on these candidate bounds determines which base algorithm to use. The approach recovers previous worst-case regret guarantees. It also provides much smaller regret in natural scenarios where some learners significantly exceed their candidate bounds. The improvement is therefore tied to the behavior of the candidate learners, rather than asserted for every possible situation.

The framework applies to nested function classes in linear bandits and Markov decision processes, unknown misspecification in linear bandits, and confidence-parameter tuning for algorithms such as LinUCB. It can also extend to adversarial contexts. These applications make the contribution a general method for allocating decisions among learning algorithms while retaining theoretical control over performance.
icml-2021-dynamic-balancing-for-model-se.tldr: A dynamic balancing rule combines candidate algorithms using possibly invalid regret bounds while retaining worst-case and scenario-dependent guarantees.

paragraphs: Invariant learning aims to identify features that remain useful when the data distribution changes, rather than relying on features tied to a particular environment. Many approaches assume training examples already have environment labels. This paper addresses the more common situation in which those labels are unavailable, making the relevant partition of the training data part of the learning problem.

EIIL combines environment inference with subsequent invariant learning. It seeks partitions that are maximally informative for the downstream learning objective. The inferred groups therefore serve a specific purpose: helping the learner distinguish environment-specific relationships from relationships that can remain useful across environments.

On CMNIST, EIIL outperforms invariant learning methods without using environment labels. On Waterbirds, it significantly improves worst-group performance over empirical risk minimization, highlighting performance for the least well-served group rather than only aggregate accuracy. The authors also connect the framework to algorithmic fairness and demonstrate improved accuracy and calibration in a fair prediction problem. These results show how inferring environments can make invariant learning useful when explicit domain annotations are absent.
icml-2021-environment-inference-for-inva.tldr: EIIL infers useful training environments without environment labels and improves reported invariant-learning, worst-group, and fair-prediction results.

paragraphs: PCA with outliers seeks a low-dimensional subspace underlying data that also contain corrupted observations. The challenge has both a recovery aspect and a computational aspect: knowing that the underlying structure can be identified does not by itself explain how difficult the required computation will be. This paper focuses on that computational question.

The authors use parameterized complexity to examine how different features of the problem affect difficulty. These include the dimension of the original data, the dimension of the desired subspace, the number and structure of outliers, and the permitted approximation error. Considering these quantities separately gives a more detailed view than treating dataset size as the only source of computational cost.

The algorithmic methods draw on randomized linear algebra and algebraic geometry. The contribution concerns fixed-parameter and approximation algorithms, organizing the search for a useful subspace around the parameters that govern the problem. Its significance is a computational perspective on robust dimensionality reduction: the structure of the instance and the accuracy requested are central parts of assessing algorithmic difficulty.
icml-2021-fixed-parameter-and-approximat.tldr: The paper studies how dimensions, outlier properties, and approximation error shape the computational difficulty of PCA with outliers.

paragraphs: Density estimation learns how probability is distributed across possible observations, without requiring labeled targets. The proposed Gradient Boosting Histogram Transform, or GBHT, brings boosting to this unsupervised task. It uses negative log likelihood as the loss, giving the boosting procedure an objective based on how well the estimated density explains the observed data.

The theoretical results depend on the smoothness of the true density. For densities in C^{0,alpha}, the authors establish fast convergence rates. Under the stronger C^{1,alpha} smoothness condition, they obtain an upper bound for GBHT that is better, in convergence-rate terms, than a lower bound for its corresponding base learner. This provides a theoretical explanation for an advantage from boosting in that setting.

The distinction matters because the result addresses whether combining learners can improve the rate of density estimation, rather than only reporting a better fitted model. The authors also compare GBHT experimentally with kernel density estimation and apply it to anomaly detection. Those experiments explore practical uses alongside the conditional theoretical account of why boosting can help.
icml-2021-gbht-gradient-boosting-histogr.tldr: GBHT uses likelihood-based boosting for density estimation and proves a convergence-rate advantage over its base learner under stronger smoothness assumptions.

paragraphs: Adversarial examples motivate a question about regularization: how does controlling a model's sensitivity relate to protecting it against changes in the data distribution? This paper develops that connection for distributional robustness defined through transportation costs. Those costs specify which distribution changes belong to the uncertainty set against which a model is evaluated.

The authors sharpen results relating this robust objective to Lipschitz regularization, which controls how sharply a function can change. They characterize conditions under which the two formulations are equal. They also tightly quantify the slack between them under assumptions described as very mild. The distinction between equality and a quantified gap is central: the paper establishes when equivalence holds rather than asserting it without conditions.

The theory is intended to accommodate broad function classes, including universal approximators. As an application, the authors derive a result clarifying the relationship between adversarial learning and distributional robustness. They additionally develop ways to impose Lipschitz regularization on kernel classifiers and demonstrate them experimentally. The work thus links a precise theoretical correspondence to a concrete regularization method.
icml-2021-generalised-lipschitz-regulari.tldr: The paper characterizes when transportation-based distributional robustness equals Lipschitz regularization and tightly bounds the gap under mild assumptions.

paragraphs: Inverse problems reconstruct an underlying image from incomplete, degraded, or compressed observations. A deep generative model can guide this reconstruction by restricting the search to images it can produce. However, optimizing only the generator's initial latent code limits the available reconstructions to those reachable through that starting representation.

Intermediate Layer Optimization progressively moves the optimization input through the generator, obtaining increasingly expressive generators. To control the search in these higher-dimensional spaces, it looks for codes within a small l1 ball around the manifold induced by the preceding layer. This gives the reconstruction additional freedom while keeping it near the structure inherited from the previous stage.

The theoretical analysis shows that keeping this radius relatively small can improve an established compressed-sensing error bound for deep generative models. Experiments report better performance than methods introduced in StyleGAN2 and PULSE across inpainting, denoising, super-resolution, and compressed sensing. The contribution combines a more flexible reconstruction search with a specific proximity constraint, supported by a conditional theoretical improvement and empirical results.
icml-2021-intermediate-layer-optimizatio.tldr: ILO expands generative reconstruction through intermediate layers while constraining each search near the previous layer's manifold.

paragraphs: Reconstructing an image from a small number of noisy measurements is important in applications such as accelerated MRI. Deep networks offer strong reconstruction accuracy, but concerns about their reliability include sensitivity to adversarial perturbations, distribution shifts, and loss of small image features. This paper investigates these concerns through comparisons across reconstruction approaches.

The evaluation includes trained neural networks, untrained neural networks, and traditional sparsity-based methods. The authors find adversarial vulnerability in both trained and untrained approaches. They also find that trained and untrained methods tuned to a particular dataset suffer similarly under distribution shifts. These observations challenge the view that the examined robustness problems distinguish learned reconstruction methods from their alternatives.

The study additionally demonstrates that a method with higher reconstruction quality performs better at recovering fine details. Taken together, the reported results indicate that state-of-the-art deep reconstruction methods can improve performance over traditional approaches without sacrificing robustness in the comparisons studied. The finding is comparative: adversarial vulnerabilities remain present, even though they do not establish a relative robustness disadvantage for the deep methods.
icml-2021-measuring-robustness-in-deep-l.tldr: Comparative tests indicate that deep image reconstruction improves quality without a robustness penalty, while trained and untrained approaches remain vulnerable.

paragraphs: An l1-bounded image attack must respect two constraints: a total perturbation budget and valid pixel values between zero and one. The paper shows that established projected-gradient attacks are suboptimal when they fail to account for the geometry of these constraints together. The actual feasible set is their intersection, so treating the image bounds as secondary misses part of the attack problem.

The authors analyze the expected sparsity of a steepest-descent step for this combined set. They show that exact projection onto it is computationally feasible and improves attack performance. They also develop an adaptive projected-gradient method that remains highly effective with few iterations, producing the white-box attack l1-APGD.

Using this stronger attack reveals that previous work overestimated l1 robustness. The authors also use it for adversarial training and report state-of-the-art l1 robustness for the resulting classifier. Finally, they combine it with an l1 adaptation of Square Attack to create l1-AutoAttack. This ensemble is presented as a reliable assessment tool for the explicitly defined intersection of perturbation and pixel constraints.
icml-2021-mind-the-box-l-1-apgd-for-spar.tldr: l1-APGD strengthens sparse adversarial attacks by jointly respecting perturbation budgets and pixel bounds, exposing overestimated robustness.

paragraphs: Distributed empirical risk minimization fits a model using data held across a network of agents. Newton methods use curvature information to accelerate optimization, but coordinating that information can be expensive. This paper develops a distributed cubic-regularized Newton method for constrained problems on an undirected communication network.

Each agent takes an inexact, preconditioned Newton step. A gradient-tracking consensus procedure estimates the gradient of the centralized loss, while the Hessian is subsampled from local data. The agents do not exchange Hessian matrices. The design therefore combines local curvature estimates with communication that coordinates the gradient estimate across the network.

For convex and strongly convex losses, the authors derive global complexity bounds that connect sample size with optimization and communication effort. Reaching statistical precision requires roughly as many iterations as centralized cubic Newton, with per-iteration communication scaling as approximately 1/sqrt(1-rho), up to the suppressed factors in the stated bound. Here rho describes network connectivity. The result improves on distributed Newton analyses that do not account for statistical precision, making the target estimation accuracy central to the computational guarantee.
icml-2021-newton-method-over-networks-is.tldr: A distributed Newton method reaches statistical precision in roughly centralized iteration counts without exchanging Hessian matrices.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns a policy from previously logged transitions without further interaction with the environment. When those records cover only a limited part of the state-action space and learning uses function approximation, the paper identifies a need to keep the policy near the logged data's support. The central question is how to define that closeness.

The authors propose an iterative procedure for learning a pseudometric from the logged transitions. This measure is closely related to bisimulation metrics and supplies the notion of proximity used by the method. They establish convergence of the procedure and extend it to function approximation, connecting the learned distance to the setting in which flexible predictive models are used.

The resulting actor-critic algorithm, PLOFF, uses a new lookup-based bonus derived from the pseudometric. This bonus encourages the actor to choose behavior close to the logged transitions according to the learned measure. Evaluations cover hand manipulation and locomotion tasks. The contribution places the choice of distance at the center of offline policy learning and turns that distance into a concrete training incentive.
icml-2021-offline-reinforcement-learning.tldr: PLOFF learns a pseudometric from logged transitions and uses it to encourage offline policies to remain close to the available data.

paragraphs: Few-shot learning tries to recognize classes from very few labeled examples. Transductive methods use the collection of examples being classified to inform their predictions, and prior work often finds them stronger than inductive alternatives. However, many transductive approaches add trainable components to an existing model, especially when built around meta-learning.

This paper introduces a transductive feature re-representation framework that adds no training parameters. It is designed to work with a broad range of few-shot methods, including both meta-learning and fine-tuning approaches. Its contribution is therefore an adaptable transformation of features, allowing existing architectures to gain a transductive component without expanding their set of trainable parameters.

The authors evaluate the framework on three benchmark datasets, applying it to representative meta-learning baselines and state-of-the-art few-shot methods. It improves performance consistently across the reported experiments and establishes new state-of-the-art results. The findings support the idea that useful transductive adaptation can come from changing feature representations, with improvements demonstrated across multiple underlying methods rather than a single specialized architecture.
icml-2021-parameterless-transductive-fea.tldr: A parameter-free transductive feature framework improves multiple few-shot learning methods across three benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Machine learning can guide compiler optimization, but useful decisions require understanding properties of programs. The authors argue that reproducing basic data-flow analyses is an important test of that understanding. If a method struggles with these foundational tasks, its ability to reason about programs is insufficient for the optimization decisions that depend on them.

The paper turns data-flow analyses into supervised learning problems and introduces a large open dataset pairing programs with analysis labels. Benchmarking existing machine learning methods on these tasks exposes their difficulties. This creates a concrete way to assess program reasoning, using targets derived from analyses that matter to compilers.

The proposed ProGraML representation expresses program semantics as graphs and is designed to be portable and independent of programming language. The authors report that it addresses limitations of earlier representations and improves performance on downstream optimization tasks. The contribution combines a diagnostic benchmark with a new representation, connecting foundational program-analysis ability to the practical goal of making better compiler optimization decisions.
icml-2021-programl-a-graph-based-program.tldr: ProGraML combines graph-based program semantics with data-flow benchmarks to improve machine learning for compiler optimization.

paragraphs: A recommender system determines which content a user has a chance to discover, as well as which items appear relevant. This paper measures that opportunity using stochastic reachability: the greatest probability that a target item could be recommended under a specified set of allowable strategic modifications. The measure makes availability an explicit object of evaluation.

Because it maximizes over allowed modifications, reachability provides an upper bound on recommendation probability rather than a prediction of how users will actually behave. The framework requires minimal assumptions about user behavior. For a variety of practical settings, the authors show that the quantity can be computed efficiently through convex optimization.

Evaluations use recommendation algorithms trained on large datasets containing explicit and implicit ratings. The results show how preference models, selection rules, and user interventions affect reachability, with effects that can be unevenly distributed. The authors also argue that reachability need not conflict with accuracy. The framework offers a way to diagnose biased content availability and restricted discovery opportunities alongside conventional recommendation objectives.
icml-2021-quantifying-availability-and-d.tldr: Stochastic reachability measures the maximum chance of recommending an item under allowed interventions, exposing uneven opportunities for discovery.

paragraphs: Submodular maximization selects a valuable collection of elements when their contributions exhibit diminishing returns. This paper studies non-negative objectives under a k-system constraint, a broad family that includes cardinality, matroid, and k-extendible constraints. The challenge is to obtain a high-value feasible selection while keeping the computation manageable.

The authors replace earlier deterministic frameworks with a randomized algorithm. Its approximation factor is (1+sqrt(k))², improving on the previous factor k+2sqrt(k+2)+3 for general submodular functions. In this convention, a smaller factor gives a stronger approximation guarantee. The algorithm also runs in nearly linear time, which the authors describe as substantially faster than the state-of-the-art alternative.

The approach extends to a stochastic setting where elements can be chosen adaptively, obtaining an approximation factor of (1+sqrt(k+1))². Experiments in data mining and social computing demonstrate advantages in both utility and efficiency. The paper therefore combines a stronger theoretical quality guarantee with a computational improvement, while carrying the randomized framework into a setting where choices can respond to observed information.
icml-2021-randomized-algorithms-for-subm.tldr: A nearly linear randomized algorithm improves approximation guarantees for submodular maximization under k-system constraints and extends to adaptive selection.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks can represent control policies whose decisions depend on internal state. One way to understand such policies is to convert them into finite-state machines and examine the resulting transitions. Earlier approaches then minimize the machine, reducing its size by merging states that can be treated as equivalent.

This paper identifies an interpretability cost of that minimization: states with different semantic meanings can be merged, hiding distinctions that help explain how the policy operates. The proposed analysis starts from an unminimized machine and applies reductions chosen to preserve key decision points. The aim is a representation that remains manageable while retaining distinctions useful for understanding behavior.

The authors also introduce an attention tool to examine the role of observations in decisions. Case studies on seven Atari games and three control benchmarks reveal insights that earlier analyses had not noticed. The contribution shows how the choice of simplification procedure affects what an analyst can learn from an extracted policy representation, even when minimizing the machine initially seems like a natural step.
icml-2021-re-understanding-finite-state-.tldr: Interpretability-focused reductions preserve meaningful decision points in finite-state representations of recurrent policies and reveal previously unnoticed behavior.

paragraphs: Adaptive cruise control must choose the gap between vehicles while accounting for traffic flow, safety, and comfort. SAINT-ACC treats these as objectives to optimize together through dynamic adaptation. The system uses deep reinforcement learning to adjust its behavior as traffic conditions change, rather than treating the inter-vehicle gap as a single fixed choice.

Its central design uses two reinforcement learning agents to seek and adapt a balance between efficiency and safety or comfort. The agents control driving-safety-model parameters and vehicle spacing using both macroscopic and microscopic traffic information. This connects information about broader traffic conditions with information relevant to individual vehicle interactions.

The evaluation comprises more than 12,000 simulation runs with varying traffic scenarios and penetration rates. In these simulations, SAINT-ACC significantly improves traffic flow, driving safety, and comfort compared with a state-of-the-art approach. These results support the proposed joint adaptation strategy across the simulated conditions examined. The evidence is specifically simulation-based, so the stated finding concerns those evaluations rather than a demonstrated deployment on public roads.
icml-2021-saint-acc-safety-aware-intelli.tldr: SAINT-ACC uses two reinforcement learning agents to adapt vehicle spacing and safety parameters, improving flow, safety, and comfort in simulations.

paragraphs: Extreme multi-label learning assigns an input a relevant subset of labels from an enormous catalog. In recommendation applications, rare labels can be especially valuable despite appearing infrequently in training. The paper focuses on using label metadata effectively and producing good predictions for these rare labels while operating at very large scale.

SiameseXML combines Siamese architectures with high-capacity extreme classifiers in a modular framework. A new probabilistic model motivates this combination, and the accompanying training pipeline scales to tasks with 100 million labels. The design brings together the two modeling components to address prediction quality and scale within the same system.

On public benchmarks, the authors report predictions that are 2–13% more accurate than those of leading extreme multi-label methods. Live A/B tests on Bing also show significant gains in click-through rates, coverage, revenue, and other online metrics over production techniques. These findings provide both benchmark and application-level evidence for the framework, supporting its usefulness beyond the ability to process a large label catalog.
icml-2021-siamesexml-siamese-networks-me.tldr: SiameseXML combines Siamese models and extreme classifiers at 100-million-label scale, with reported benchmark and live recommendation gains.

paragraphs: This paper constructs a distribution transformation through a sequence of greedy steps. Each step applies optimal transport along one-dimensional slices, matching their marginal distributions to the target. The orthogonal slice directions are selected to maximize the current distributional difference measured by Wasserstein distance, helping the method address high-dimensional data.

The authors introduce two versions of sliced iterative normalizing flows. GIS maps from data to latent space, while SIG maps in the reverse direction. This separates density-estimation and generation uses within the same iterative framework. The training procedure does not use mini-batching, stochastic gradient descent, or backpropagation through deep layers, distinguishing its construction from the usual end-to-end approach.

SIG generates image samples whose quality matches the GAN benchmarks in the reported evaluation. GIS is competitive with density-trained normalizing flows on density estimation and, on small training sets, is faster, more stable, and achieves higher p(x). These results support greedy slice-wise transport as an alternative way to build expressive distribution models, with different empirical strengths in generation and density estimation.
icml-2021-sliced-iterative-normalizing-f.tldr: Sliced iterative flows use greedy one-dimensional transport steps for competitive image generation and density estimation without deep backpropagation.
